title: Formula G

source.quote: Con + Gimmick = Response -> Switch -> Crossup -> Payoff

setting: Two weeks into a rough sprint. Mei has quietly taken on everyone's overflow work, always with the same bright "I've got it, don't worry about it."

L1.line: No one appreciates what I do around here!
cues: this is the third weekend she's stayed late
L1.question: Mei has spent two weeks quietly taking on everyone's overflow work. This is the line that makes the room go quiet. Which stage of Formula G is this?

options.feedback: Not quite - the Con was the quiet non-verbal offer two weeks ago ("I've got it, don't worry"), and this line comes well after it. This moment is actually the Switch: the instant Mei's role flips from quietly helping to accusing everyone of not noticing - the floor-moving moment this whole formula is built to catch.

Not quite - the Gimmick belongs to whoever bought into the Con (here, the teammates who let her take the work), and this line is Mei's own. This moment is actually the Switch: the instant her role flips from quietly helping to accusing everyone, the floor-moving moment this whole formula is built to catch.

Not quite - the Response was the two weeks of her actually doing the extra work while everyone said "thanks, you're a lifesaver"; this line breaks that pattern instead of continuing it. This moment is actually the Switch: the instant her role flips from quietly helping to accusing everyone, the floor-moving moment this whole formula is built to catch.
Right. This is the Switch: the moment the role flips, Rescuer becomes accusing Victim, mid-sentence, and everyone in the room feels the floor move.

Close, but not quite - the Crossup is the beat right after this (the stunned "wait, what?" on everyone's faces); this line causes the Crossup, it isn't the Crossup itself. This moment is the Switch that triggers it: the instant Mei's role flips from quietly helping to accusing everyone, the floor-moving moment this whole formula is built to catch.

Not quite - the Payoff lands after the Crossup, once the racket feelings settle (Mei's grim satisfaction, the team's guilt); this line is a step earlier, the thing that triggers all of that. This moment is the Switch: the instant her role flips from quietly helping to accusing everyone, the floor-moving moment this whole formula is built to catch.

L1.lesson: Formula G runs Con + Gimmick = Response -> Switch -> Crossup -> Payoff. The Switch is the diagnostic moment: the instant a role flips and both players feel the floor move. Everything before it can look like an ordinary helpful pattern; the Switch is what proves it was a game.

L2.intro: Two weeks of "I've got it, don't worry about it" from Mei. Tonight she's still at her desk at 7pm, and you're about to leave.

beats.line: It's fine, I've got it. Go home, don't worry about it.
cues: this is the third extra task this week
the bright tone doesn't match the stack of files

options.outcome: Mei beams, tired. The stack doesn't shrink, and your gratitude just bought her another week of it.
options.lesson: Taking the help at face value and praising it is the Gimmick's payoff for her Con - it feels good for both of you right now, and it's exactly what keeps the Response stage running.

options.text: Are you sure? That's the third thing this week.
options.outcome: Mei pauses. "I mean... yeah, I guess it is a lot." For a second the performance drops.
options.lesson: Naming the pattern out loud, from Adult, is the earliest point anyone can catch a game - right at the Gimmick, before the Response stage even gets going properly.

options.outcome: You leave. Mei stays. Nothing is said, nothing changes.
options.lesson: Not feeding the game isn't the same as interrupting it - staying neutral lets the Response stage run exactly as long as it was always going to.

beats.line: No one appreciates what I do around here!

options.text: That's not fair, we never asked you to do all that.
options.outcome: "Oh, so now it's MY fault for trying to help?" Mei fires back. The fight is officially on.
options.lesson: Meeting her Victim-to-Persecutor flip with your own Persecutor just trades which corner of the Triangle each of you stands on - the game continues, now louder.

options.text: You're right, we should've appreciated you more, I'm sorry.
options.outcome: Mei softens, but files the apology away as proof she was right to feel unappreciated. Next sprint, she volunteers for everything again.
options.lesson: Comforting the Victim role confirms it was the right role to take - kind in the moment, and it reloads the same game for next time.

options.text: Sounds like you've been doing a lot nobody signed up for. What do you actually want to happen now?
options.outcome: Silence. Then: "...I don't actually know. I just know I'm exhausted." First honest sentence of the conversation.
options.lesson: This is the Switch's real exit: cross to Adult instead of taking the Victim or Persecutor role on offer, and ask the concrete question instead of supplying the expected reaction - this is what stops a Switch from completing into a Payoff.

fields.label: Write Mei's game in one sentence per stage: Con, Gimmick, Response, Switch, Crossup, Payoff.
Name Mei's Drama Triangle role before the Switch, and after. What role did Dev almost take by reacting instead of asking?

echo.setting: Three days later. Mei is already reaching for someone else's task before they've finished asking.
echo.line: It's fine, I've got it, don't worry about it.
